k-1.x_notes: Strengths: very concrete; children actually play games from 4, 5, 7-9 and 12 counters with a partner, and all the mathematics is correct (3 is a trap; from 7 go first and take 1, from 8 take 2, from 9 go second). The header and footer with an id are in the right format. Weaknesses: it gives the thinking away. Problem 4 says 'choose your reply so that exactly 3 counters remain', and Problem 6 says 'take enough to remove 3 counters between your two turns', so the multiple-of-3 strategy is handed over instead of discovered. The full rules are restated in Problems 1, 3 and 5. Much of the work is copying moves into boxes, which is slow and empty for kindergartners, and 'Draw the two groups' is busywork. There are only six thin problems on one idea, with no rule change and no second game, which is exactly the dumbed-down, too-short K-1 page the organizer complains about. Pages are half empty.
k-1.y_notes: Strengths: the rules are stated once, then there are ten well-sequenced problems with large counter pictures children can circle or match with real counters. The sequence runs from piles 1-5 (take to win, or cross out), to who wins from 6-9, to 10-12, to 'trap' defined and every trap marked to 20, to Ben's forced first move, to listing every way a 4- or 5-counter game can go (the 5 and 8 rows exactly match the 5 and 8 sequences), to rule {1,2,3}, to two piles (including a non-obvious (1,4) second-player win), to the copy/mirror strategy with 6+6, to misere. All answers check out. Nothing gives the strategy away, and there is real development and contrast across rules. Weaknesses: no explicit prompt to play, although play is implied and counters are on the table. Traps to 20 and the two-pile and misere problems will need adult support for kindergartners. Problem 9 has no recording space. The footer has no id, and the last page is mostly blank.
k-1.reason: Y gives K-1 real, varied mathematics with usable counter pictures and lets children find the traps themselves. X is thin, wordy, and prints the multiple-of-3 strategy as a direction, which removes the discovery.

grades-2-3.x_notes: Strengths: correct analysis of {1,3,4} (L at 0, 2, 7, 9, 14). Hands-on building and play from small piles. Problems 5 and 6 ask for every winning move from 8 and from 10 (10 has two, take 1 or take 3). Problem 4 tests a losing pile against every first move. Weaknesses: Problem 3 prints the backward-induction rule as a procedure ('Mark W if at least one is L; mark L if all are W'), and Problem 4 then gives the answers away ('such as 2 or 7'). The work is broken into tiny directed steps ('Reset each time', 'Record...'), and the chart stops at 7 to 10. There is no repeating pattern, no rule change, and no claim to judge beyond its own chart. The rules are restated, and it reads like a filled-in procedure rather than an investigation. It may run short for strong third graders.
grades-2-3.y_notes: Strengths: shared rules stated once. Problem 1 warms up with {1,2}. Problem 2 tests Lee's mirror-to-3 claim (correct) and Mo's 'take 2 from 10' (wrong, because 8 remains), which matches the outline's 'test claimed strategies against every reply'. Problem 3 checks Jo (leaving 7 is a trap, and children trace every reply to the end) and Kai (leaving 8 is beatable by taking 1). Then the children classify 1-20 under {1,3,4} and extend the pattern to 30, 50, 61 and 100 (30 and 100 are losses; from 50 take 1; from 61 take 3). After that come {1,3,5} parity with an explanation, two piles (including (4,1), a second-player win), inventing rules that make the multiples of 5 losing ({1,2,3,4} or e.g. {1,2,3,4,6}), and misere {1,3,4} (L at 1, 3, 8, 10, 15, 17). All of it is correct, open and well sequenced, with generous space. Weaknesses: little explicit direction to play with counters. Problem 5 (up to 100) and Problem 8 stretch second graders and need adult support. The footer has no id.
grades-2-3.reason: Y develops the {1,3,4} classification, claim-testing, rule change and pattern extension with open, correct problems. X hands children the induction rule and even the L piles, so it reduces the session to filling in tables.

grades-4-5.x_notes: Strengths: the mathematics is correct throughout. It reaches the real periodicity argument in Problems 9 and 10: the next label depends on cells 1, 2 and 4 of a four-label window, and the windows at 0 and 7 match. It includes some play (8, 10, 14; 24 counters; {1,3,5}). The footer has an id. Weaknesses: it heavily gives away the discovery. The chart is laid out in rows of seven with 'Compare the rows', Problem 5 says to arrange the counters 'in whole groups of 7', and the window-sliding rule is printed as a procedure, so children carry out the proof instead of finding it. Instructions are fussy or unclear: Problem 6's 'use piles 7 and 9 so that all three moves are possible', and Problem 8's 'check a proposed strategy' when no strategy has been proposed. The rule change is barely explored, there is no comparison across several rules, the greedy move is never examined, and there are no sums of games. The rules are restated.
grades-4-5.y_notes: Strengths: rich and open throughout, and every answer checks out. Children classify {1,3,4} to 24 (L at 2, 7, 9, 14, 16, 21, 23), then decide 100 (losing), 1000 (take 4) and 2026 (take 1 or 3). They compare four rule sets: {1,2} and {1,2,4} both give multiples of 3, {1,4} gives remainders 0 and 2 mod 5, and {1,3,5} gives even piles. They test the greedy plan, which fails in {1,2}, {1,3,4} and {1,4} and always works in {1,3,5}, and they explain why the pattern must continue forever. Problem 6 asks for every subset of 1-6 whose losing piles are the multiples of 4, with a completeness proof (answer: {1,2,3} plus any of 5 and 6). Then comes misere, a two-pile {1,2} grid, and a two-pile {1,3,4} grid whose answers (1,3), (1,8), (3,8), (2,7), (4,6) lead toward Grundy values without naming them. Weaknesses: largely pencil-and-paper, with no explicit play prompt. The proof problems need adult guidance. The footer has no id. Probably more than 40 minutes of work, which is acceptable here.
grades-4-5.reason: Y covers all three kernels with contrasting rules, a test of the greedy move, a real classification-and-proof problem and two-pile sums, all correct and open-ended. X reaches periodicity only by printing the groups-of-7 structure and the window procedure for children to follow.

overall.reason: In every band Y has more mathematics, better sequencing and correct, open problems. X consistently prints the intended discovery as directions (the groups of 3 at K-1, the W/L rule and the L piles at 2-3, the groups of 7 and the window procedure at 4-5). Y needs only small edits (footer ids, perhaps a line inviting play with counters), while X would need restructuring that cannot be done in fifteen minutes per band.
